content.content:
1	# Issue #230 — a web control surface on the remote port: investigation notes
2	
3	Worktree: `/Users/sbgragent/.dispatch/worktrees/299903e5`, HEAD `7fe8949` (Release 0.4.1), branch `dispatch/230-…`.
4	Read: CLAUDE.md (system-supplied copy), `docs/design.md` (remote status §3107, trust boundary §219), `docs/lessons.md`, `docs/remote-client.md` §§3–5, 10–13 (§4.1–4.4 read in full), `src/adapters/remote.rs` (1–560, 586–660, 765–880, 960–976), `src/app.rs` (remote regions), `src/core/remote.rs`, `src/ports/remote.rs` (1–150), `src/ui/remote.rs`, `control/src/lib.rs` (SessionView), `src/ui/cards.rs` (caption and excerpt), `client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift`, `client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift`, `tests/remote.rs` (names and helpers), `Cargo.toml`. Nothing was run and nothing was edited.
5	
6	## 1. The surface the page would sit on
7	
8	**Routing and responses.** `serve_remote` (`src/app.rs:3017`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/` prefix with a 404 JSON `not_found` (`src/app.rs:3023`). That refusal runs on the frame, so every stray `GET /` costs a frame pass and an unauthenticated slot. Only `GET /api/v1/info` and `POST /api/v1/pair` are answered before authentication (`src/app.rs:3028-3029`). `respond` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:530-553`) writes `Content-Type: application/json` unconditionally (line 545) and has no way to add headers. `RemoteReply` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:389-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}` with no headers field, so neither `Set-Cookie` nor a CSP can leave the port today.
9	
10	**Request parsing.** `read_request` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:444`) keeps the query, the `Authorization: Bearer` value (line 487), and `Upgrade` with `Sec-WebSocket-Key` (line 491). It discards `Cookie`, `Origin`, `Sec-Fetch-*`, `User-Agent` and `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. Nothing checks `Host`.
11	
12	**WebSocket.** `respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) writes a 101 with no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. The upgrade's bearer check runs in `serve_remote` before `remote_subscribe` (`src/app.rs:3036-3037`, `authenticate` at `src/app.rs:3127`). A refused upgrade gets the JSON error as a plain HTTP response, which a browser's WebSocket object cannot read.
13	
14	**TLS.** `tls_config` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:144-155`) sets no ALPN, so a client falls back to HTTP/1.1. The certificate is made with `rcgen::CertificateParams::new(vec![])` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:102`): no subject alternative names, a common name of `Switchboard <server_id>`, and rcgen's default far-future `not_after` (per the doc comment at line 91).
15	
16	**Pools and limits.** `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:567-568`). The accept loop drops a stranger past the pool at once (`src/adapters/remote.rs:701-706`). A connection starts in the unauthenticated pool and moves to the paired pool only on its first authenticated reply (`src/adapters/remote.rs:835-845`). After the first request the read timeout is `IDLE_TIMEOUT = 30 s` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:573`), so a keep-alive connection holds its slot for up to 30 s after its last request. Rate windows cover only the exact paths `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`src/adapters/remote.rs:583-586`, `631-639`).
17	
18	**Pairing.** `remote_pair` (`src/app.rs:3606`) checks the body's `spki_sha256` against the host's (`src/app.rs:3636`) before the code (`src/app.rs:3646`). A wrong key or a wrong code each count against the global window (`PairingFailed`). The success reply is a JSON body carrying the token in clear (`src/app.rs:3660-3665`), with `scope`, `server_id` and `device_id`. The token is stored only as its SHA-256 (`src/core/remote.rs:166` `new_device`). The window is single use (`src/core/remote.rs`, the `Paired` arm closes `self.pairing`). The device name is the body's `device_name`, trimmed to 64 characters, default `"Device"` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`, `src/core/remote.rs:166-174`).
19	
20	**Refusals and logs.** `refuse` (`src/app.rs:3754-3772`) logs method and path, not the query, so the `code` in `?code=` is not logged on a refusal. The `authenticate` refusals for a missing bearer and for an unknown token share the code `unauthorized` (`src/app.rs:3127-3152`). The page therefore cannot tell "revoked" from "never paired" from the code.
21	
22	**Scope.** `GET /api/v1/info` (`src/app.rs:3568-3599`) returns identity, `capabilities` (line 3580), limits and `pairing_open`. It does not return the caller's scope, and no endpoint does. A read device sending a command gets 403 `scope` (`src/app.rs:3166-3173`). The only place a page could learn its scope is the pair reply body.
23	
24	**Send.** `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/send` takes `{op, text}` (`src/app.rs:3179`, `3192`), with `text` capped at `SEND_BYTES_CAP` (16 KiB) and `op` at 64 characters. Command routing is `remote_command` (`src/app.rs:3159`).
25	
26	**Pairing window UI.** `pairing` (`src/ui/remote.rs:141`) builds the QR payload at lines 160-165 as JSON `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`. `addresses` holds the single result of `remote::local_address()` (`src/ui/remote.rs:157`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:962-969`, an IPv4 UDP-connect trick). The text form is the same JSON, copied by "Copy invite" (`src/ui/remote.rs:201-205`). The QR is a `qrcode` texture (`src/ui/remote.rs:280`).
27	
28	**A tree fact the QR does not reflect.** `bind_remote` listens on loopback unless `identity.listen.lan` is set (`src/app.rs:2962-2966`). The pairing window does not check that: it always prints `local_address()` (`src/ui/remote.rs:157`), so with LAN off the QR names an address the listener does not answer. The plan has to decide whether opening the window requires LAN.
29	
30	## 2. What is stored, and how the port rehydrates
31	
32	**On disk.**
33	- `identity.json`: `Identity` (`src/ports/remote.rs:26`) with `server_id`, `server_name`, the DER certificate, `spki_sha256`, `created`, `listen`. It has a `schema_version` field but the device file does not.
34	- The private key is a Keychain item under `remote-key:<server_id>` (`src/ports/remote.rs` `key_account`).
35	- `devices.json`: a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96`; `load_devices` returns the vec with `unwrap_or_default`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-82`). Fields: `id`, `name`, `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen` (`#[serde(default)]`). Adding a field needs `#[serde(default)]` on it; there is no version to bump.
36	- Session records, projects, sets and so on: the app's existing store. The port reads them through `AppCore` and never writes them.
37	
38	**What a browser device adds to disk.** One more `PairedDevice` row: a name, a scope, the token's hash, times. The token itself is never stored. The cookie or the header the browser keeps lives only in that browser. The name is the only new data; a user-agent-derived name would be a string the device supplies, trimmed and capped at 64 characters, as today.
39	
40	**Rehydration on the host.** On launch the core reads `identity.json` and `devices.json` (`IdentityLoaded`, `src/core/remote.rs`), and the port binds when the key is present (`bind_remote`). Session state comes back from the store in the usual `StoreLoaded` then `HostListed` reconcile. The port's epoch is per run, so a host restart changes `epoch` and every client refetches.
41	
42	**Rehydration in the page.** The page holds nothing that survives a visit except what it stores itself. The tree gives it no store:
43	- the token, if it is kept at all, lives where the decision in §3 puts it;
44	- the host's key, for an "identity changed, pair again" comparison on a later visit. Nothing in the tree stores a key for the page, and `/info` only gives the current one. A page reopened without a code therefore has no earlier key to compare against unless the plan stores it somewhere (localStorage, IndexedDB, or a cookie). The issue does not say where.
45	
46	So a reopened page rehydrates by `GET /api/v1/info`, then the reads it needs, then the events socket with subscribe-then-snapshot (`docs/remote-client.md` §4.4). The page's own state is UI state, not a read model (§12.6).
47	
48	## 3. What the pane shows, and what the tree lacks for it
49	
50	**The list.** `GET /api/v1/projects`, `GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/sessions`, `GET /api/v1/waiting` exist (`src/app.rs:3040-3060`). `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637-678`) carries `kind`, `liveness`, `card` (a state word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `trust_question`, `name`, `project`, `last_stop_at_ms`, `quiet_secs` and `last_activity_ms`. Grouping by project, waiting first and marked, is possible with what is there.
51	
52	**The excerpt is not on the wire.** The issue asks for "the one-line excerpt the card shows". In the tree the card's excerpt is computed in the UI: for Claude Code sessions it is `agent_excerpt(conversation)` (`src/ui/cards.rs:558-574`), a function of the parsed transcript; for other kinds it is the caption or the host title (`src/ui/cards.rs:176-180`). `SessionView` has no excerpt field. `docs/remote-client.md` §4.4 and §4.3 name a `last_message` from the `Stop` hook as a metadata field, but `grep` finds no such field in `control/src/lib.rs` or the port. The excerpt would need either an additive wire field computed in the core (CLAUDE.md: logic under `ui/` moves to the core; `docs/lessons.md`, "Keep `ui.rs` dumb"), or one `last-response` fetch per Claude session.
53	
54	**The session view.** `GET /api/v1/sessions/{id}/last-response` is served (`src/app.rs:1967`, routed at `src/app.rs:3101`), and `GET .../screen?lines=` is served by the same route family (`src/app.rs:1947`). A Claude session's response is `last-response`; anything else uses `screen`. Both are masked before they are cut (the redaction policy in `docs/remote-client.md` §4.3 and `remote_content_route`, `src/app.rs:1947-2024`).
55	
56	**The reply.** `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` (`src/app.rs:3179-3192`). The page can make `op` a UUID and send it again only on a timeout, which follows §4.5.
57	
58	**Live updates.** `changed {kind,id}` for `session`, `sessions`, `waiting`, `conversation` and `screen` are emitted by the read-model diff (`src/core/revision.rs`, which the file list in design.md names, and the port's events). A session that starts waiting therefore produces `changed {waiting}` and the page refetches the collection, as the issue asks.
59	
60	**The "device's scope" in the header.** The page can show the host name from `/info`. It cannot show the device's scope from any endpoint (see §1, Scope). If the plan keeps only a cookie, it needs an endpoint or a field for the caller's scope, or it has to store the scope from the pair reply and accept that a dialog change does not reach the page until a refusal.
61	
62	**"Revoked".** A revoked device gets `401 unauthorized` with "the token is not known; pair again" (`src/app.rs:3142-3148`), the same code as a device that never paired (`src/app.rs:3129-3135`). The page would need a distinct code. A revoked device's WebSocket is closed (`docs/remote-client.md` §4.5, and the `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket` test in `tests/remote.rs:2891`), and a browser WebSocket cannot read a refused upgrade's body (see Open questions).
63	
64	## 4. The pairing URL and the native text path
65	
66	- `PairingInvite` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift`, the `parse` function at the end of the file) decodes JSON only (`Wire.decode`). A URL form needs a second parser on the Swift side, and the CLI's one-argument `pair` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift`, the `pair` branch, `rest.count == 1`) calls it directly.
67	- `client/Tests/SwitchboardProtocolTests/FixturesTests.swift:158-164` tests the JSON invite from an inline string, not from `client/Fixtures/`. No invite fixture exists in `client/Fixtures/` (its 28 files are reply bodies such as `pair.json` and `info.json`).
68	- `tests/remote.rs` drives the port with a raw TLS client (`http()`, `tests/remote.rs:245-297`, `Host: localhost`, pinned through `pinned_client`), and `pair()` (`tests/remote.rs:406`) posts `/pair` with the JSON body. The `crate::adapters` module is public (`src/lib.rs:19`), so a test can reach the page constants.
69	- The URL's `key` parameter matches `spki_sha256` in `/info` and the `/pair` body. Both are checked by the host already (`src/app.rs:3636`), so the page's own comparison adds a refusal before the code is sent, not a second trust check.
70	- The refusal logs carry method and path only (`src/app.rs:3754-3772`), so `?code=` is not written to the log by the port. Nothing else in the port logs a request line.
71	
72	## 5. Dependencies and rules the plan has to respect
73	
74	- `Cargo.toml` has `tungstenite 0.30`, `rustls` (ring), `rcgen`, `base64`, `qrcode` (no default features), `rustix`, `getrandom`, `sha2`, `uuid`, `serde_json`. No cookie or user-agent crate. A cookie parser or UA name mapping would be hand-written, or added as a dependency with a CI check.
75	- `web/` does not exist in the tree. The `include_str!` files and a route table would be new.
76	- CLAUDE.md: the `unsafe` ban and the Linux CI rule apply to any new code. The embedded page is not egui, so the UI-test rule in CLAUDE.md does not cover it; `tests/remote.rs` does.
77	- CLAUDE.md "Adding a feature" wants an action variant and core test, an effect for the outside world, and README and design.md updates. A static route is adapter-only, and a `CHANGELOG.md` line under Unreleased is required for a user-visible change.
78	- The trust-boundary paragraph in `docs/design.md` (around line 219-262) would need the page's sentence, as §5 of `docs/remote-client.md` already says.
79	- CLAUDE.md asks for a spike directory before building on a new risky mechanism. A browser's handling of a self-signed certificate, cookies and WebSockets on it is one, which is why it is listed below as a run-or-source question.
80	- Redaction is unaffected: the page reads through the same content routes. Static files carry no session data and do not need the redaction path.
81	
82	## 6. Which decisions the tree already settles, and which it leaves to the plan
83	
84	Settled by the tree (the plan should cite, not re-decide):
85	- Auth for every non-static read is the bearer, checked in `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127`), and the token is stored only as its hash (`src/core/remote.rs:166`).
86	- `/pair` already refuses a key that is not the host's (`src/app.rs:3636`) before the code is checked.
87	- A WebSocket subscription needs `Upgrade` and a bearer (`src/app.rs:3036-3037`, `src/app.rs:2723`).
88	- Pools: 4 unauthenticated, 12 paired, rate windows only on `/pair` and `/info`.
89	
90	Left to the plan (design choices, not open questions here): the cookie vs. subprotocol choice for the token; the click-through trust step; one QR or two; the static path table and headers; which pool a page load counts against; the device name's source; the excerpt field; the scope endpoint; the distinct revoked code; the LAN requirement for opening the pairing window; where the page keeps a pinned key.
91	
92	## 7. What I did not check
93	
94	- I did not run the host, the tests, or any browser. Nothing here is measured.
95	- I did not read `src/adapters/remote.rs` 560–765 and 880–1088 beyond their names (the subscriber loop, `serve`'s pools in detail, the tests), nor `src/app.rs` beyond the remote regions I listed, nor `src/core/revision.rs`, the watch set, the content cache, or the worker.
96	- I did not read the Swift transport (`SwitchboardTransport`), the pinning delegate, `client/Fixtures/*.json` contents, or the visionOS app.
97	- I did not read `spikes/22-remote-port` beyond its file list and the design's summary of its results.
98	- I did not confirm the event kinds from the diff code or the tests; `docs/design.md` and `tests/remote.rs` names say they exist.
99	- I did not check `scripts/bundle.sh`, the README's dev-aid list, or the CHANGELOG format.
100	
101	## Open questions
102	
103	- [source] Whether Chrome, Safari on macOS, and Safari on iOS/iPadOS let a user click through the warning for a self-signed certificate with no subject alternative name, a common name only, and a far-future expiry, when the host is an IP address.
104	- [source] Whether the click-through exception covers `wss://` and `fetch` to the same host and port, and whether it persists after the browser is closed and reopened, per browser.
105	- [source] Whether any browser lets a page pin a certificate's SPKI hash for `fetch` or `WebSocket` on an origin (the issue says none does).
106	- [source] Whether the WHATWG WebSocket constructor can send custom headers (the issue says it cannot; the constructor takes only a URL and protocols).
107	- [source] Whether any published specification (RFC 6455, WHATWG Fetch or Cookies) forbids a token in a URL, or whether the prohibition is this repo's own rule in `docs/remote-client.md` §5.
108	- [source] Whether `Set-Cookie` with `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` set from an https origin on an IP-address host is stored after a certificate click-through, in each browser.
109	- [source] Whether `SameSite=Strict` cookies are sent with a WebSocket handshake and with `fetch` from the same origin, and whether a page on another origin on the same host (a different port, or a rebinding name) makes a credentialed request that carries them.
110	- [source] Whether browsers send `Origin` and `Sec-Fetch-Site` on WebSocket upgrades, and which values a cross-port same-site request carries, since the port would need an `Origin` check if a cookie carries the token.
111	- [source] Whether a 101 without `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` is accepted by a browser that offered a protocol, which decides whether a subprotocol-carried token works.
112	- [source] What a WebSocket `error` event exposes to script on a refused upgrade (status, body), since the revoked state needs the body.
113	- [source] Whether `history.replaceState` removes the code from the back-forward cache, the session restore data and the Referer of later requests, in Safari and Chrome.
114	- [source] Whether `connect-src 'self'` permits the same origin's `wss:` URL in Safari and Chrome, and whether `script-src 'self'` with no inline script is enough for the page's load.
115	- [source] How many connections a browser opens for one page load and its WebSocket, and whether Safari on iOS/iPadOS and Chrome send `/favicon.ico` or `apple-touch-icon.png` unprompted, since four unauthenticated slots are shared by them.
116	- [source] Whether a browser retries or reports a failed page load when the host closes an accepted connection past the pool (the accept-time drop at `src/adapters/remote.rs:701`).
117	- [source] Whether iOS and iPadOS Safari's user agent says `iPhone` or `iPad` for the device, or reports a desktop `Macintosh` form on iPad, which decides how a `Safari on iPhone` name can be derived.
118	- [source] Whether Chrome or Safari's Local Network Access permission prompts when a page served from a LAN address fetches from that same address.
119	- [run] The browser's real connection count and request order for one page load, against the port with a stub page, to see whether the 4 unauthenticated slots are reached before pairing.
120	- [run] Whether `history.replaceState` before the first `fetch`, a cookie set through a click-through, and a WebSocket upgrade on a self-signed certificate all work end to end in one browser on this Mac.
121	- [run] Whether `switchboard-remote pair` with a URL argument, once the parser exists, pairs against a host with `lan` on, and with `lan` off (the loopback case in §1).
122	- [owner] On a phone, whether the iOS Camera opens a QR's https URL in Safari directly, and what the warning looks like there.
123	- [owner] On the owner's network, whether the address `local_address()` picks is the one the phone can reach (several interfaces, a VPN).
124	- [owner] Whether a click-through the owner makes once is acceptable as the only trust step on a home network for a device with `control` scope.

# Spikes

Throwaway crates and scripts that answered the Spike 0 questions in
`docs/design.md` before any product code was written. Each directory has a
README with the commands run, their output, and a recommendation. They are
kept for reference and are not built by the main crate.

| Dir | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `01-claude-resume` | Can Claude Code sessions be captured and resumed? | Yes: `--session-id <uuid>` at launch, `--resume <uuid>` later from any terminal. Transcripts pruned after 30 days unless `cleanupPeriodDays` is raised. |
| `02-process-host` | tmux or own PTYs? | tmux on a private server: sessions outlive the app, reattach works, ~3 ms round trip. PTY adapter kept as fallback and for tests. |
| `03-session-state` | How to know "waiting on you"? | Claude Code hooks (`PermissionRequest`, `Stop`, `SessionEnd`) via a tiny `switchboard-hook` binary and a Unix socket; OSC 777 text from the raw stream as the hook-free fallback. |
| `05-keychain` | Can secrets live in the Keychain without prompts? | Yes for a bundle signed with a stable identity and identifier: the item ACL is `identifier + certificate`, so rebuilds read silently. Ad-hoc builds prompt per rebuild. |
| `06-pane-size` | Why is the embedded pane wider than the widget? | `window-size manual` ignored the client; `latest` makes the window follow whichever client attached last. Re-applied on launch for servers that outlive the app. |
| `07-clone-session` | Can a session be cloned up to a chosen message? | Yes: copy the transcript prefix before the chosen prompt, substitute a fresh UUID for `sessionId`, save it `0600` beside the original; `--resume <new>` opens the truncated history and the original is untouched. |
| `08-promptbox-embed` | Can Prompt Box be the agent message box? | Yes: same egui 0.36, drawn into a bottom panel unchanged, a `Clipboard` adapter turns Send into a hand-off; needs an embedded mode, a sink port, and focus-scoped shortcuts in promptbox. |
| `09-popout` | Can a session live in a window of its own? | Yes: an immediate viewport drawn from the main frame holds the page, terminal, and side panel; its frame is saved to settings and restored. |
| `10-nunchuk-serial` | Can a nunchuk drive the working set over USB serial? | Yes: one line per button change or stick flick from the Feather, read on a thread that reconnects; round trip 2 to 9 ms. Firmware in `firmware/nunchuk`. |
| `11-gate-sandbox` | Can Dispatch's pipeline commands be confined to the ticket's tree on macOS? | Yes: `sandbox-exec` with `(allow default)`, writes denied except the tree, the attempt directory, the lane's caches and a base set; ~5 ms start-up; a refused write is `EPERM` and a tagged `deny(1)` line in the unified log. `setuid` programs and keychain creation fail inside it. |
| `12-hidden-frames` | Does the frame loop keep running while the window is occluded or minimized? | Not before the fix: with the app hidden, a control query timed out after 10 s and was answered at once on unhide. With the tick and `pump` in `App::logic`, hidden queries answer in 75 to 103 ms (eframe's 100 ms throttle for invisible windows). The sleep and wake cycle is not yet measured. |
| `13-dispatch-service` | Can a Dispatch service be a Switchboard service session, and how is its port read? | Yes: `$SHELL -lc 'exec "$@"' dispatch-service env PORT=<port> npm start` finds `npm`, answers (CRA in 27 s), and is gone with its port 200 ms after `kill-session`. A port is free only if `0.0.0.0`, `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` all bind: CRA listens on `*`, which a loopback bind does not see. |
| `14-env-exec` | Do a pane's record id and launch token reach a child, so `switchboard-env exec` can resolve its sets? | Yes for a shell grandchild of a tmux pane started with `-e`; the binary's path is covered by `tests/control.rs`. The `aws-vault` form and the no-prompt run under Dispatch's launch flags were not run and are left to the owner. |
| `15-paste-buffer` | Can a multi-line send be bracketed only for a pane that asked for it? | Yes: `load-buffer -` then `paste-buffer -p -r -d` frames the text in `ESC[200~` .. `ESC[201~` for a pane with `bracket_paste_flag` 1 and delivers it bare otherwise; `-r` keeps LF, `-d` leaves no buffer. CR passes through and tmux 3.7c shows ESC as a literal `^[`, so the sender turns CR into LF and removes ESC. `send-keys -H` passes the markers to every pane. Measured on tmux 3.7c. |
| `16-base-pipeline` | Can Dispatch find a merged pull request's merge commit and read the base's pipeline on it? | GitHub, yes: `mergeCommit` on `gh pr list` and `gh pr view`, and the commit's `check-runs` (a short hash works) show the base's run in progress and then finished. Bitbucket's reads were not run (the token could not be read in the run); the adapter follows the documented `merge_commit.hash`, commit `statuses` and pipeline `steps`, with a read by number when a list row lacks the commit; until they are run, a wait on a Bitbucket base pipeline is refused. |
| `18-tmux-argv` | Do `new-session -e` values show in a process listing, and can they reach tmux another way? | Yes, they did: the server keeps the argv of the client that started it. `tmux start-server \; source-file -` with the `new-session` line on stdin keeps every value and the pane command off any argv; cold and warm both work, errors still return, and double-quoted values with `\n` for line breaks round-trip (single quotes lose a line starting with `#`). Measured on tmux 3.7c. |
| `19-structured-ask` | Does a card's answer to a structured ask reach interactive Claude Code as the next user message, sent once, both at the prompt and when held until the turn's `Stop`? | Yes: `Owner answered "<question>": <answer>`, typed as one line, arrived as its own user message once in both cases; a held answer went out only after the `Stop`. Measured on Claude Code 2.1.293 by the ignored gate test `a_structured_answer_arrives_as_the_next_prompt`. |
| `21-evidence-writes` | Which writes reach a stage's evidence directory, outside the agent's cwd, without a prompt? | The Write tool, under the attempt directory's `Edit(//<dir>/**)` rule. Bash `cp`, `mv` and `mkdir` ask, and `--add-dir` does not change that. A Playwright MCP screenshot is refused outside the server's roots unless it runs with `--allow-unrestricted-file-access`. Measured on Claude Code 2.1.295 and `@playwright/mcp@0.0.82`. |
| `22-remote-port` | Can a pinned-TLS HTTP and WebSocket port run on std with every request answered by the frame thread, and what does it cost? | Yes: `rustls` + `rcgen` + `tungstenite` + `mdns-sd`, no Tokio; the frame's share is under 0.25 ms per pass, latency is one frame interval, the pools and the subscriber overflow hold under a stall and an unread socket, Bonjour is seen by `dns-sd`. A 146 MB transcript parses in 290 ms at 575 MB peak, so content work leaves the frame thread. ctime and inode see the file changes mtime and size miss. |
| `04-terminal-view` | Embedded terminal or hand-off? | Hand off agents to Ghostty (`open -na Ghostty --args ... -e cmd`, raise by title); embed `egui_term` for shells, commands, services. |

Findings are folded into `docs/design.md` under "Spike 0 results".

entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.

Web search results for query: "WebSocket constructor cannot set custom headers Authorization browser WHATWG Sec-WebSocket-Protocol token"

Links: [{"title":"- From: Martin Altenstedt <martin.altenstedt@gmail.com>","url":"https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-webapps/2015JanMar/0340.html"},{"title":"websocket authentication","url":"https://blog.openreplay.com/websocket-authentication/"},{"title":"blog.4d.com","url":"https://blog.4d.com/?p=51438"},{"title":"injecting custom data in websocket client headers","url":"https://blog.4d.com/injecting-custom-data-in-websocket-client-headers"},{"title":"community.auth0.com","url":"https://community.auth0.com/t/how-do-you-securely-pass-a-token-over-websocket-with-auth0/120247"},{"title":"websocket header atuh","url":"https://apidog.com/jp/blog/websocket-header-atuh"},{"title":"docs.flashphoner.com","url":"https://docs.flashphoner.com/x/fopfAQ"},{"title":"discourse.wicg.io","url":"https://discourse.WICG.io/t/headers-support-for-websocket-upgrade-request/1575"},{"title":"Updated 2x","url":"https://dev.library.kiwix.org/content/stackoverflow_en_nopic_2021-08/questions/4361173/http-headers-in-websockets-client-api"}]

The search didn't return the WHATWG spec text itself, but several sources cover the constraint and the common workarounds.

**The constraint:** Browsers don't let page code set arbitrary headers on a WebSocket handshake. A W3C mailing-list proposal from 2015 asked for an optional third constructor argument for headers, because a bearer token is sent in the Authorization request header field for OAuth-protected servers, and the WebSocket API gives no way to set request header fields. A WICG discussion makes the same point and argues that the RFC 6455 doesn't prohibit custom headers, so the limitation appears to be browser-only.

**The Sec-WebSocket-Protocol workaround:** The constructor's second argument is the only way to influence the handshake beyond the URL. One answer notes that the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header, which is sometimes extended for WebSocket-specific authentication, is generated from that optional second argument. A common pattern is to request a short-lived ticket over HTTP and then pass it through the URL, the protocol field, or the first message after connecting. The server then accepts the connection only if the ticket is valid.

**Other options:** The OpenReplay guide lists three approaches: a token in the query string, a cookie the browser attaches automatically, or a credential sent in the first message. It also notes that a token valid at handshake time can expire or be revoked while the socket stays open. A query-string token is the simplest option, but it can leak into logs, so one Auth0 community thread calls it not secure.

**Legacy note:** Basic-auth credentials in the URL were once used to generate an Authorization header, but modern browsers no longer send that header.

Non-browser clients such as Node.js can set headers directly, so the restriction applies only to browser code.

Web search results for query: "SameSite=Strict cookie sent with WebSocket handshake same-site cross-port Origin header check cross-site WebSocket hijacking"

Links: [{"title":"GHSA 2vfc 3h43 vghh","url":"https://github.com/Syslifters/sysreptor/security/advisories/GHSA-2vfc-3h43-vghh"},{"title":"Cross-site WebSocket hijacking: understanding and exploiting CSWSH","url":"https://pentest-tools.com/blog/cross-site-websocket-hijacking-cswsh"},{"title":"Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking Exploitation in 2025","url":"https://blog.includesecurity.com/2025/04/cross-site-websocket-hijacking-exploitation-in-2025/"},{"title":"gorbe.io","url":"https://gorbe.io/docs/owasp/go-scp/communication-security/websockets"},{"title":"Cross-Site Websocket Hijacking (CSWSH)","url":"https://praetorian.com/?p=694"},{"title":"Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking Explained: How Attackers Abuse WebSockets and How to Defend Against It","url":"https://hackmag.com/security/websocket-csrf"},{"title":"cross site websocket hijacking cswsh","url":"https://praetorian.com/blog/cross-site-websocket-hijacking-cswsh"},{"title":"cross site websocket hijacking cswsh","url":"https://git.koelner.dedyn.io/coelner/hacktricks/blame/branch/master/pentesting-web/cross-site-websocket-hijacking-cswsh.md"},{"title":"# Cross-site WebSocket hijacking (CSWSH)","url":"https://git.koelner.dedyn.io/coelner/hacktricks/raw/branch/master/pentesting-web/cross-site-websocket-hijacking-cswsh.md"}]

The search turned up consistent guidance, though nothing that directly addresses cross-port behavior.

- **SameSite=Strict doesn't block same-site WebSocket handshakes.** A SysReptor advisory describes a server that skipped Origin validation on WebSocket connections but used SameSite=Strict session cookies. The browser still sent those cookies on the cross-origin handshake because the request was same-site, so the attack was limited to malicious same-site subdomains ([GHSA-2vfc-3h43-vghh](https://github.com/Syslifters/sysreptor/security/advisories/GHSA-2vfc-3h43-vghh)).
- **The Origin check is the primary defense.** One guide says the server should verify the handshake's Origin and fail the handshake if it isn't trusted ([Include Security](https://blog.includesecurity.com/2025/04/cross-site-websocket-hijacking-exploitation-in-2025/)). RFC 6455 leaves that check to the application, so the protocol doesn't enforce it ([Praetorian](https://praetorian.com/blog/cross-site-websocket-hijacking-cswsh)).
- **Prerequisites include a non-Strict cookie.** The same Include Security guide lists cookie-based auth, a SameSite=None cookie, and no Origin validation as the usual conditions for CSWSH ([Include Security](https://blog.includesecurity.com/2025/04/cross-site-websocket-hijacking-exploitation-in-2025/)).

On your cross-port question: the search didn't address it. From general knowledge (not these results), a site is defined by scheme and registrable domain, and ports are ignored. So a page on a different port of the same host counts as same-site, and a SameSite=Strict cookie would be sent on its WebSocket handshake. Only the Origin check (which does include the port) would distinguish it. Please verify this against the spec or browser documentation before relying on it.

Links: [{"title":"Hello All,","url":"https://community.graylog.org/t/graylog2-https-error-on-chrome/2936"},{"title":"SNI certificates - Doesn't seem to work with LuCI and TLS","url":"https://forum.openwrt.org/t/sni-certificates-doesnt-seem-to-work-with-luci-and-tls/11053"},{"title":"nethserver.org","url":"https://community.nethserver.org/t/chrome-58-doesnt-work-with-nethserver/6730"},{"title":"community.atlassian.com","url":"https://community.atlassian.com/forums/Jira-questions/JIRA-Chrome-58-SSL-Security-missing-subjectAltName/qaq-p/581668"},{"title":"Netgate Discussion Forum","url":"https://forum.netgate.com/topic/124567/certificate-problem-err_cert_common_name_invalid-in-chrome"},{"title":"Webgui Https error NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID","url":"https://www.truenas.com/community/threads/webgui-https-error-net-err_cert_common_name_invalid.56087/post-392804"},{"title":"Webgui Https error NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID","url":"https://www.truenas.com/community/goto/post?id=392789"},{"title":"Webgui Https error NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID","url":"https://www.truenas.com/community/goto/post?id=393264"},{"title":"SSL warning: NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID","url":"https://kb.metricinsights.com/m/52384/l/745836-ssl-warning-net-err_cert_common_name_invalid"}]

The search turned up consistent explanations from several forums and a Metric Insights support article.

**Cause:** Chrome 58 (April 2017) stopped using the Common Name field for hostname matching. One forum post puts it this way: Chrome looks only to the subjectAlternativeName field. A certificate with an IP address only in the CN therefore fails, even if it's self-signed. The same error appears when the certificate lacks a SAN entry at all, as the Graylog thread shows with its "missing subjectAltName" message ("The certificate for this site does not contain a Subject Alternative Name extension containing a domain name or IP address").

**Fix:** The usual answer is to regenerate the certificate with the IP in the SAN field. One Netgate user was told to use either FQDN or IP address, not a made-up hostname. An OpenSSL example from the forum threads adds a `subjectAltName` entry under the v3 extensions section, with `IP.1` set to the server's address. Metric Insights likewise says the solution is to re-generate the certificates to include a Subject Alternative Name extension.

**Proceeding past the warning:** Users who want to skip the check can click through Chrome's Advanced option and choose to proceed. One user reported that with the exception rule [ADVANCED -> Proceed to … (unsafe)] their self-signed certificate worked. This only bypasses the warning for that browser and doesn't fix the certificate. Another option is to install the self-signed certificate or its CA in the trusted root store, though one user who did this still hit the error until they reissued the cert with a SAN.

Sources: Graylog community forum, OpenWrt forum, NethServer forum, Atlassian community, Netgate forum, TrueNAS community, and Metric Insights knowledge base. Most of these are user reports rather than official documentation, and the dates range from 2017 onward.

**Cause:** Chrome 58 (April 2017) stopped using the Common Name field for hostname matching. One forum post puts it this way: Chrome looks only to the subjectAlternativeName field. A certificate with an IP address only in the CN therefore fails, even if it's self-signed. The same error appears when the certificate lacks a SAN entry at all, as the Graylog thread shows with its "missing subjectAltName" message ("The certificate for this site does not contain a Subject Alternative Name extension containing a domain name or IP address").

**Fix:** The usual answer is to regenerate the certificate with the IP in the SAN field. One Netgate user was told to use either FQDN or IP address, not a made-up hostname. An OpenSSL example from the forum threads adds a `subjectAltName` entry under the v3 extensions section, with `IP.1` set to the server's address. Metric Insights likewise says the solution is to re-generate the certificates to include a Subject Alternative Name extension.

**Proceeding past the warning:** Users who want to skip the check can click through Chrome's Advanced option and choose to proceed. One user reported that with the exception rule [ADVANCED -> Proceed to … (unsafe)] their self-signed certificate worked. This only bypasses the warning for that browser and doesn't fix the certificate. Another option is to install the self-signed certificate or its CA in the trusted root store, though one user who did this still hit the error until they reissued the cert with a SAN.

Sources: Graylog community forum, OpenWrt forum, NethServer forum, Atlassian community, Netgate forum, TrueNAS community, and Metric Insights knowledge base. Most of these are user reports rather than official documentation, and the dates range from 2017 onward.

The search turned up a few relevant points, though none is a definitive spec citation for browser behavior.

- **Browsers restrict failed-handshake details on purpose.** In the noVNC issue, a maintainer explained that for security reasons, WebSocket error statuses are fairly restricted to limit the ability of malicious JS to probe an internal network. That is why the `error` event usually gives you no status code.
- **Some browsers do log the status in the console.** A commenter on the same issue said that in Chrome, if the connection closes before the handshake, an error with the code appears in the log, for example a 404 "Unexpected response code" message. Your code can't read that value from the event, though.
- **Failed handshakes don't produce a close code.** An UnexpectedServerResponse-style failure happens when the server returned a status code other than 101, is missing required headers, or is not configured to handle WebSocket connections at all.
- **The standards discussion is unsettled.** A 2011 W3C public-webapps thread asked which events should be fired when WS(S) connection establishment fails for cases like unreachable hosts and TLS failures. The thread doesn't give a final answer.
- **TLS failures may show up as code 1015.** Dart's library documents that code as the connection was closed due to a failure to perform a TLS handshake. It also notes that this code must not be set explicitly by an endpoint.

**Practical takeaway:** Browser JavaScript generally can't see the HTTP status or the reason for a pre-handshake failure. The usual workarounds are to check the browser console or network tab, test the endpoint with a non-browser client such as curl, or have the server expose the failure reason through a separate HTTP endpoint.

The search turned up a known Safari limitation, with workarounds that vary by iOS version.

- **Root cause:** Safari doesn't carry a user's manual certificate exception over to WebSocket connections. A 2011 WebKit mailing-list thread describes the same pattern: this will fail in Safari and WebKit (r87480.) Chrome, by contrast, consider the user's acceptance of the server's identity as valid for both wss:// and https:// connection.
- **Certificate requirements (iOS 13+):** A Cendio bug report found that iOS 13 has some new requirements on certificates, and that adding a Subject Alternative Name was the critical missing piece. The same report lists Extended Key Usage and validity period as other requirements the certificate must meet.
- **Error to look for:** A Turris project saw OSStatus Error -9807, which corresponds to an invalid certificate chain.
- **Recent reports:** An Apple Developer Forums post from iOS 26 Beta 3 describes The certificate for this server is invalid. even after the page loaded over https with the certificate accepted. This suggests the problem persists on newer releases.
- **Workarounds:** Cockpit's documentation says a valid certificate is the real fix, and suggests an alternative: enable Apple's future/experimental WebSocket framework which does work as expected. On iOS, that is under Settings > Safari > Advanced > Experimental Features as "NSURLSession WebSocket."

Practical takeaway: regenerate the certificate with a SAN matching the hostname or IP, Extended Key Usage set to serverAuth, and a validity period under current Apple limits. Otherwise, use a certificate from a trusted CA or enable the experimental WebSocket flag for testing. I couldn't confirm the current exact limits from these results, so check Apple's TLS certificate requirements page before relying on specific numbers.

Safari on iPadOS has sent a macOS-style user agent since iPadOS 13, so user-agent sniffing alone can't reliably tell an iPad from a Mac.

- **Default desktop UA:** Safari for iPad presents itself as Safari for Mac on all iPad models by default. A developer forum example shows the iPad string matching the Catalina Mac string, with only the Version token differing. This means it is now impossible to detect an iPad as an iPad through User-Agent analysis alone.
- **Exception:** Slide Over is the exception, since Mobile Safari is still set as the user agent there.
- **Desktop-site mode:** When a user picks Request Desktop Site, it drops the Mobile token, which leaves the iPad indistinguishable from macOS Safari in server logs.
- **Detection workaround:** Developers commonly check touch support instead. One forum post notes that navigator.maxTouchPoints returns 5 on an iPad and 0 on a desktop. A commonly shared fix combines the platform check with a test for a Mac user agent plus touch-event support (`"ontouchend" in document`).

Caveats: these sources mostly date from the iPadOS 13 era (2019–2020), and I didn't find current information on whether Apple has changed this behavior since. Verify against current iPadOS behavior before relying on it. Feature detection (touch points, pointer events) is generally more dependable than UA parsing.

content.content:
**Bug:** WebKit bug 158345 reports that secure WebSocket (`wss://`) connections don't send a client certificate, so the TLS handshake fails. The server log shows the failure as "peer did not return a certificate." The reporter saw this in a WebKit nightly on macOS.

**Context:** The reporter's test setup used a self-signed server certificate. One commenter found that Safari and Chrome only accepted it when it included a Subject Alternative Name, and that the WebSocket worked only after a normal page load and manual certificate acceptance in the UI.

**Cause:** WebSockets run in the Network process through CFStream, which has no client-certificate handling. Regular page loads get certificate challenges through a callback, but CFStream needs the certificate configured up front.

**Status (as of the last update, July 2021):**
- Still NEW and unassigned, with priority P2 and normal severity.
- A full fix would mean reimplementing WebSockets on NSURLSessionStreamTask. Alex Christensen called this a substantial change with high regression risk.
- Apple has an experimental "NSURLSession WebSocket" option under Develop → Experimental Features. Users report it works for some sites, but one reported that it worked only until the page was refreshed, and another reported that it broke WebSockets on Big Sur and iOS 14 betas due to a per-message deflate bug.

content.content:
**Constructor parameters:** The spec defines `new WebSocket(url, protocols)` with only two parameters. There is no `options` parameter. `url` is a string using the `ws`, `wss`, `http`, or `https` scheme. `protocols` is an optional string or array of subprotocol names, defaulting to an empty array.

**Custom headers:** The spec does not let scripts set custom headers. The user agent sets the handshake headers itself, including `Upgrade`, `Connection`, `Sec-WebSocket-Key`, `Sec-WebSocket-Version`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, and `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions`. Cookies are handled through Fetch with credentials mode set to "include."

**Handshake failure:** If the handshake fails, the spec runs "fail the WebSocket connection," which closes the connection and fires a `close` event. An `error` event fires only if the user agent was required to fail the connection, or if the connection closed after being flagged as full. The `close` event has `wasClean` set to false and `code` set to 1006. The spec also says:

- "User agents must not convey any failure information to scripts" in a way that would reveal the cause, such as DNS failure, a refused connection, or a TLS error. So the error event does not include failure details.

**Subprotocol mismatch:** If `protocols` is non-empty and the server's `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` response is missing, malformed, or empty, the connection fails. The spec notes this differs from the RFC check: "This covers a subprotocol requested by the client, but not acknowledged by the server." Separately, the constructor throws a `SyntaxError` if a protocol value is duplicated or invalid.

content.content:
**1. "Same-site" and ports**

The draft does not say whether port matters for same-site. It defers to another specification: "Two origins are same-site if they satisfy the "same site" criteria defined in [SAMESITE]." (Section 5.2)

It also defines a registrable domain in Section 2.3 but does not mention ports there.

**2. SameSite=Strict behavior**

- Section 4.1.2.7: "If the "SameSite" attribute's value is "Strict", the cookie will only be sent along with "same-site" requests."
- Section 5.6.7.1: "Same-site cookies in "Strict" enforcement mode will not be sent along with top-level navigations"

**3. Secure attribute and secure contexts**

- Section 4.1.2.5: "The Secure attribute limits the scope of the cookie to "secure" channels (where "secure" is defined by the user agent)."
- Section 5.7, step 13: "If the request-uri does not denote a "secure" connection (as defined by the user agent),"

The draft leaves "secure" to the user agent to define, so it does not explicitly tie this to secure contexts.

**4. __Host- prefix requirements**

- Section 4.1.3.2: "the cookie will have been set with a `Secure` attribute, a `Path` attribute with a value of `/`, and no `Domain` attribute."
- Section 5.7, step 21 applies the same requirements as a storage rule, with the host-only-flag also required to be true.

**5. Whether cookies are scoped by port**

Cookies are not isolated by port. Section 1 says: "cookies for a given host are shared across all the ports on that host, even though the usual "same-origin policy" used by web browsers isolates content retrieved via different ports."

Section 4.1.3.2 adds: "Ports are the only piece of the origin model that `__Host-` cookies continue to ignore."

The search turned up a long-standing spec gap, but nothing confirming whether Safari has fixed it recently.

- **The spec behavior:** A WebKit bug report says 'self' in connect-src does not match the web socket scheme as per spec, and it was later marked as a duplicate of another bug. The reporter noted that Chromium had the same issue and fixed it earlier.
- **Browser differences:** One 2019 commenter verified that it exists in Safari but works as intended (by the specification) in Chrome and Firefox. A 2021 comment on the same bug said it was still not fixed in Safari 14.
- **Root cause:** A W3C CSP issue from 2015 shows that declaring the 'self' source will not allow websockets back to the same host, because the scheme differs and so the origin differs. The maintainer's response at the time was that this is the specified behavior.
- **MDN's current note:** MDN says connect-src 'self' does not resolve to websocket schemes in all browsers.
- **Common workaround:** Projects add an explicit scheme source. One OpenBMC commit adds 'wss:' to connect-src directive in CSP to fix Safari WebSocket console errors. A Coder commit notes that its extra ws/wss sources exist to support old webkit based browsers (Safari). See issue: w3c/webappsec-csp/issues/7.

**Caveat:** The Safari reports I found date from 2019 to 2021. I couldn't confirm whether current Safari versions still have this behavior, so test in your target Safari version. If it still fails, add explicit `ws:` and `wss:` sources (or the specific host) alongside `'self'`.

The search returned mostly Chrome's June 2025 announcement of Local Network Access. It doesn't directly address your case, a page served from a private IP fetching that same address, so treat the points below as partial.

**What the sources cover:**
- Chrome is adding a permission prompt for sites that connect to a user's local network. The aim is to protect users from cross-site request forgery attacks against routers and other private-network devices, and to limit fingerprinting of the local network.
- Chrome treats a request as local-network traffic when the hostname is a private IP literal such as 192.168.0.1, when the hostname ends in .local, or when the fetch call sets the targetAddressSpace option to "local". The listed cases are a private IP literal, a .local hostname, and a fetch() annotated with targetAddressSpace: "local".
- A public domain that resolves to a private address is not automatically classified as local. The example fetch to example.com is not exempt, even if that domain resolves to a local network address.
- Early opt-in testing started in Chrome 138 through a flag, chrome://flags/#local-network-access-check set to "Enabled (Blocking)".
- Chrome's older Private Network Access rules add preflight requests, and the preflight response must include Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network: true. The same post says devices need new response headers to support the prompt, namely Private-Network-Access-Name and Private-Network-Access-ID (devices must include two new response headers, Private-Network-Access-Name and Private-Network-Access-ID).

**Gap:** Nothing in these results says whether a page served from 192.168.x.x and fetching 192.168.x.x triggers the prompt, or whether same-origin or same-address requests are exempt. For that, search the Local Network Access spec (WICG) or Chrome's current Private Network Access documentation, and check the current Chrome release notes, since this area has changed since 2025.

The search confirmed the standard `Sec-Fetch-Site` values, but it did not directly confirm how this header behaves on WebSocket handshakes or whether `Origin` is always sent.

- **Valid values:** The header takes one of four values: cross-site, same-origin, same-site, and none. Cross-site means the initiator and the server have different sites, and same-site means they share a site, including the scheme, without needing the same origin (same scheme, host and port). The "none" value covers user-initiated actions, such as typing a URL into the address bar (entering a URL into the address bar, opening a bookmark, or dragging-and-dropping a file into the browser window).
- **Your query's term is off:** A ZAP scanner rule lists "cross-origin" as a valid value (same-origin, same-site, cross-origin, or none). That does not match the MDN spec values above, so I'd treat it as a scanner error rather than a real value.
- **WebSocket mode:** The `Sec-Fetch-Mode` header has a websocket value, which indicates the request is being made to establish a WebSocket connection. That is useful evidence that browsers send fetch metadata on WebSocket handshakes, but the results don't say whether `Sec-Fetch-Site` is included alongside it.
- **Origin header:** None of the results address whether browsers always send `Origin` on WebSocket handshakes. Check the WebSocket spec (RFC 6455) or browser documentation for that.

Links: [{"title":"How to modify a URL without reloading the page with vanilla JavaScript","url":"https://gomakethings.com/how-to-modify-a-url-without-reloading-the-page-with-vanilla-javascript/"},{"title":"Remove query string result in referrer tracking | Community","url":"https://experienceleaguecommunities.adobe.com/adobe-analytics-3/remove-query-string-result-in-referrer-tracking-92910"},{"title":"wiki.suikawiki.org","url":"https://wiki.suikawiki.org/n/pjax$12573"},{"title":"wiki.suikawiki.org","url":"https://wiki.suikawiki.org/n/Pjax$12573"},{"title":"Remove query string result in referrer tracking | Community","url":"https://experienceleaguecommunities-beta.adobe.com/adobe-analytics-3/remove-query-string-result-in-referrer-tracking-92910"},{"title":"• During processing of a shortcode, my plugin reacts to a URI query string","url":"https://wordpress.org/support/?p=14054399"},{"title":"kiwix.org","url":"https://dev.library.kiwix.org/content/stackoverflow_en_nopic_2021-08/a/22753103"},{"title":"the history interface","url":"https://arai.searchfox.org/firefox-main/source/testing/web-platform/tests/html/browsers/history/the-history-interface"},{"title":"twinery.org","url":"https://twinery.org/forum/discussion/comment/4234"}]

The search turned up useful material on using `history.replaceState` to strip query strings, but nothing specific on Safari's back-forward cache or session restore.

- **Stripping the query string in place:** One tutorial removes a tracking parameter with `URLSearchParams.delete()` and then calls `history.replaceState(history.state, '', url.href)` to update the visible URL without a reload. The displayed URL is updated so the parameter is no longer visible to visitors.
- **Splitting on "?":** Several answers suggest taking the part of the URL before the question mark, for example `location.href.split("?")[0]`, and passing that to `replaceState`. One WordPress thread labels this approach untested. The thread offers history.replaceState(null, "", location.href.split("?")[0]) as a fix, which the poster flags as untested.
- **Referrer caveat:** One Adobe Analytics thread points out that checking the current URL is not the same as checking the referrer, and replacing a specific string is not the same as removing everything after the query. That suggests `document.referrer` needs separate handling, and the scrubbed URL won't change what the browser already sent.
- **Referrer header behavior:** The Firefox web-platform test index includes tests for history.pushState/replaceState and referer headers, which is the most direct source here on how the Referer header relates to these calls. I did not open the tests, so I can't say what they assert.
- **Browser behavior:** A Stack Overflow mirror notes that Firefox seems to ignore a pushState call with an empty string as the URL, and adding a slash worked as expected. Treat this as a cross-browser caution, not a Safari finding.

I did not find anything on Safari's back-forward cache or session restore. Those would need a separate search, such as the WebKit bug tracker or WebKit blog posts on bfcache.

The search mostly covered the click-through warning and self-signed certificates in general. It did not address the cookie or secure-context parts of your question, so those points below are unverified.

**What the results cover:**
- Chrome shows a warning for self-signed certificates because it can't verify the issuing authority. The reason for this warning is that Chrome / Chromium cannot verify the certificate that UCS offers. The browser does not know the CA that is used by UCS to sign the certificate.
- Bypassing it is a per-session workaround. In one case, the user still had to accept the Chrome warning on first access after closing Chrome or after a reboot or logout.
- Trust can be made permanent by importing the certificate. One guide says to type chrome://settings/certificates in your browser's address bar, then import the file and check the box to trust it for identifying websites.
- IP-address certificates need the address in the Subject Alternative Name field. One guide shows adding IP.1 = 123.123.123.123 to the config before generating the certificate.

**What the results don't cover:**
- Whether cookies with the Secure attribute are stored or sent when the page is reached through the "Proceed" exception on an IP address.
- Whether such a page counts as a secure context.

From my own knowledge, not these sources: Chrome treats the page as HTTPS after the bypass, so Secure cookies are probably set, and Chrome's secure-context rules generally cover HTTPS origins regardless of certificate trust. Chrome also treats localhost as potentially trustworthy, but I'm not aware of an equivalent exemption for bare IP addresses. Verify these with Chrome DevTools (Application → Cookies, and `window.isSecureContext`) or the Chromium source before relying on them.

content.content:
- **When it triggers:** The prompt appears for public-to-local requests made via `fetch()`, subresource loading, and subframe navigation, when the Chrome 138 flag is set to "Enabled (Blocking)." Requests from service or shared workers require the origin to have already been granted permission.

- **Locally served pages fetching their own origin:** The page doesn't address this directly. It defines the first milestone as covering requests "from the public network to a local network or loopback destination," so local-to-local requests appear out of scope for now. The search didn't confirm that the fix shipped enabled by default in Safari 15. The results show the NSURLSession WebSocket path was still an experimental flag, and a 2020 bug comment says the work was ongoing.

- **Bug history:** WebKit bug 158345, open since 2016, traces the problem to Safari's WebSocket implementation. Engineers in 2018 said a proper fix would mean reimplementing WebSockets on a different stream API, which was a large, risky change. In April 2020, a WebKit engineer said work was underway to use the NSURLSession WebSocket API, with an early version in Safari Technology Preview under Develop → Experimental Features. The experimental feature can even be enabled in the already released Safari 13.1 and in iOS 13.4.1.
- **Current workaround guidance:** The Cockpit documentation says Safari's default WebSocket framework on iOS, iPadOS, and ARM-based Macs does not support the WebSocket Secure sessions which Cockpit needs to function when using a self-signed or otherwise invalid certificate, even when they are manually marked as trusted. It recommends enabling the experimental "NSURLSession WebSocket" option as an alternative, or installing a valid certificate.
- **Trust-based workaround:** A Priint vendor article, tested on Safari 15.6.1, describes adding the certificate to Keychain and setting it to "Always trust" so wss connections work. It also notes that if the certificate changes, the trust must be removed and redone.
- **Historical context:** A 2010 WebKit bug report (41419) showed that Safari did not honor manual trust for self-signed wss certificates even after the certificate was added to the keychain. Once the certificate was set to "always trust," the connection worked.

I did not find a source stating that NSURLSession WebSocket became the default in Safari 15, so that part of your premise remains unverified. A search for the WebKit release notes or the bug 158345 resolution status would settle it.

# Facts for #230 (web control surface)

No spike was run. The one question the plan turns on (Safari's `wss://` after a click-through) has a source that settles its shape, and its exact current behaviour needs an iPhone, so it goes to the owner. Tree questions are answered by the investigation's file and line references and are not repeated here.

## Settled

**1. A browser's `WebSocket` cannot set headers. Its only handshake inputs are the URL and subprotocol names.**
- WHATWG WebSockets: `new WebSocket(url, protocols)`, no options argument. https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/#the-websocket-interface
- MDN: "constructor accepts only `url` and `protocols`". https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket/WebSocket
- Queries: "WebSocket constructor cannot set custom headers Authorization browser WHATWG Sec-WebSocket-Protocol token".

**2. A subprotocol-carried token needs the host to echo one offered protocol.**
- If `protocols` is non-empty and the 101 omits `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, the browser fails the connection. The spec says this "covers a subprotocol requested by the client, but not acknowledged by the server". (WHATWG, above.)
- RFC 6455 §4.2.2: the server's value must be one the client offered, or null. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-4.1
- `respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) writes no such header today, and `read_request` drops `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` (investigation §1). That option needs both changed.

**3. A script sees nothing of a refused upgrade: no status, no body.**
- WHATWG: user agents "must not convey any failure information to scripts". The `close` event reports `wasClean=false`, `code=1006`. MDN agrees that the `error` event carries no documented properties.
- The page cannot learn "revoked" from the socket. It must make a `fetch` (e.g. `/info` or a read) and read that 401. The refusal needs a code distinct from "never paired" (`src/app.rs:3129-3148`, both `unauthorized` today).
- Queries: "WebSocket error event no information on failed handshake status code browser security".

**4. Browsers send `Origin` on every WebSocket handshake. The server has to check it.**
- RFC 6455 §4.1: the request "MUST include" `Origin` "if the request is coming from a browser client". §4.2.2: "If the server does not validate the origin, it will accept connections from anywhere", and the server may answer 403.
- `read_request` drops `Origin` today (investigation §1). Any cookie-authenticated socket needs it kept and compared to the host's own `https://<host>:<port>`.

**5. `SameSite` does not isolate ports. A cookie carries to a page on another port of the same host.**
- RFC 6265bis §1: "cookies for a given host are shared across all the ports on that host". §4.1.3.2: "Ports are the only piece of the origin model that `__Host-` cookies continue to ignore". https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html
- The draft defers "same-site" to another spec and does not say port, so `Strict` crossing ports is not stated there. It is not needed: the cookie is host-scoped either way.
- Consequence: another local service on the same address could trigger a credentialed request to this port. The `Origin` check in (4) and a custom request header on `fetch` (not CORS-safelisted, so it forces a preflight the host does not answer) are what close this. `SameSite` does not.
- The Sec-Fetch-Site values (`same-origin`, `same-site`, `cross-site`, `none`) are in MDN; whether `Sec-Fetch-Site` is sent on WebSocket handshakes was not found. Do not rely on it. (Queries: "SameSite=Strict cookie sent with WebSocket handshake same-site cross-port Origin header check cross-site WebSocket hijacking"; "Sec-Fetch-Site header WebSocket handshake Origin header always sent...".)
- The SysReptor advisory GHSA-2vfc-3h43-vghh reports the same pattern: `SameSite=Strict` cookies sent on a same-site WebSocket handshake with no Origin check.

**6. "No token in a URL" is this repo's rule, not a standard's.**
- `docs/remote-client.md:312` ("never in a URL") and `:318` ("keep tokens out of logs, URLs, ..."). RFC 6455 does not forbid it. Sources recommend against it for log leakage (OpenReplay, Auth0 thread). That is a lead, not a standard.
- The plan keeps the rule and the spec amends nothing there.

**7. Chrome ignores the common name. A certificate with no subject alternative names fails hostname matching for a bare IP.**
- Chrome 58 (2017) dropped CN matching. Error `ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID`: "does not contain a Subject Alternative Name extension containing a domain name or IP address". The Advanced > "Proceed (unsafe)" click-through still exists for it, per several user reports.
- This is user reports only (Graylog, NethServer, Atlassian, Netgate threads); I did not reach Chromium's own page. By the standard in the brief it is one source type, but no source contradicts it, and it agrees with the investigation's cert facts (`src/adapters/remote.rs:102`, empty SAN list).
- Queries: "Chrome self-signed certificate IP address no subjectAltName ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID proceed unsafe".
- The plan should add the listen address as an IP SAN to the generated certificate. That changes the SPKI only if the key changes, so existing pins hold if the key is kept. Regenerating the certificate with the same key keeps `spki_sha256`; confirm in the plan against `identity.json`'s stored DER.

**8. Safari's `wss://` does not honour a certificate click-through. This is the plan's main constraint.**
- WebKit bug 158345 (open since 2016, still NEW at the July 2021 last update): WebSockets run on CFStream and have no challenge callback. A full fix means reimplementing on NSURLSession, called "substantial" and risky. https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345 . WebKit bug 41419 is the original report. Apple's "NSURLSession WebSocket" experimental feature is the workaround.
- Cockpit documents the current behaviour: Safari's default WebSocket framework on iOS, iPadOS and ARM Macs "does not support the WebSocket Secure sessions" with self-signed certificates "even when they are manually marked as trusted"; the options are the experimental flag or a valid certificate. https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari (undated; the page's footer runs to 2026). A vendor article tested on Safari 15.6.1 says that adding the certificate to Keychain as "Always trust" makes `wss` work.
- An Apple developer forum post from iOS 26 beta 3 reports "The certificate for this server is invalid" for a page that had loaded over https after acceptance (seen in search results, not opened).
- Queries: "Safari iOS self-signed certificate warning ... WebSocket wss fails after accepting certificate"; "WebKit Safari WebSocket self-signed certificate exception not honored wss NSURLSession WebSocket fixed enabled by default Safari 15".
- Consequence for the plan, which holds whatever the owner reports: the page must work without the socket. It polls `GET /api/v1/...` on a timer when the socket does not open, and it uses the socket where it does. Chrome is said to accept the exception for `wss` (the 2011 WebKit list thread, a lead), but I have no current source, so the polling path is the floor for every browser.
- The route that makes `wss` work on Safari is trusting the certificate on the device (the issue's "download it" alternative), which needs a SAN (7) and, on iOS, the profile-install and trust steps. Both routes have to be written down by the plan, with the click-through only reaching the page and REST.

**9. A CSP `connect-src 'self'` may not cover `wss:` in Safari.**
- WebKit bug 201591: `'self'` does not match the WebSocket scheme. A 2021 comment says still unfixed in Safari 14; MDN notes the same ("does not resolve to websocket schemes in all browsers"). Projects add `wss:` explicitly (OpenBMC, Coder). W3C CSP issue #7 is the spec history.
- Plan: `connect-src 'self' wss://<host>:<port>` is not knowable at compile time. Use `connect-src 'self' wss:` or build the header from the request's `Host` on a validated value. The first is simpler. Whether current Safari still needs it is not settled (latest evidence 2021).
- `script-src 'self'` with no inline script is the standard CSP; I found nothing contradicting it, and it is a CSP basics claim, not browser-specific.

**10. iPadOS Safari reports a Mac user agent by default.**
- Apple Developers forum thread 119186 and MacStories: since iPadOS 13, Safari for iPad sends the desktop Mac string; only Slide Over keeps the Mobile token. `navigator.maxTouchPoints` is 5 on iPad and 0 on a Mac.
- Data is from 2019 to 2020. A name from the user agent alone cannot say "iPad". The page can send `maxTouchPoints` in the body with the device name, or the plan accepts "Safari on Mac" for an iPad. No other source gives more.

**11. Chrome's Local Network Access prompt does not apply to a page fetching its own address, and does not gate WebSockets yet.**
- The prompt covers requests "from the public network to a local network or loopback destination"; local-to-local is out of scope for now and the page plans to extend later. WebSocket is a listed known gap. Prompt "launching in Chrome 142". https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access
- A page served from the LAN address itself is local to local, so no prompt in Chrome as of 142. Safari's rule was not searched.

**12. `history.replaceState` changes the URL the page reports; it cannot recall what was already sent.**
- The scrubbed URL is what later requests use as the Referer, since a request's referrer comes from the document URL at request time. This is from general knowledge, not a fetched source: treat as Unresolved for the strict claim.
- The search turned up only how-to pages, nothing on back-forward cache or session restore (queries: "history.replaceState remove query string Referer referrer-policy fragment safari back-forward cache session restore URL").
- Plan regardless: serve the page with `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, and call `replaceState` first. The URL also exists in the camera app's history and in the browser's history entry for the load itself, which `replaceState` replaces in place but a server cannot control. The plan should say so in the paired-devices dialog and keep the five-minute single-use window as the real bound.

## Unresolved

**U1. Whether the Cookie route works on a click-through address in each browser (`Secure` cookie stored from a certificate-exception origin; `HttpOnly` sent on `fetch`).**
- Tried: "Chrome certificate exception 'Proceed to' self-signed cookies Secure attribute stored IP address https secure context". Results covered the warning only, not cookie storage.
- Favourable: the `/pair` reply sets `__Host-`-style `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/` and the plan keeps the token out of script. Unfavourable: the page keeps the token in `localStorage` and sends it as the bearer header on `fetch`, and polls (see 8). The plan must build the host so both work: accept the cookie and the bearer, and have the page choose by feature test, whichever the owner's answer. Do not wait on this line.

**U2. Whether Chrome's click-through covers `wss://` and persists across restarts.**
- Tried: queries in 8. Only the 2011 WebKit list thread says Chrome treats acceptance as valid for both; it is old. Build to the polling floor from 8; if favourable, the socket is an upgrade on Chrome, never a requirement.

**U3. Whether any browser can pin an SPKI hash for page `fetch`/`WebSocket`.**
- Not searched with a result: I found nothing that provides it (Expect-CT and public key pinning headers are removed from Chrome; I did not fetch a source). Plan on none. The `key`-in-URL comparison is a check against `/info`, which an impostor serves too; the plan words it as a guard against a mistyped or stale address, not an authentication step.

**U4. Connections per page load and whether browsers fetch `/favicon.ico` or `apple-touch-icon` unprompted.**
- Not searched with a result. Plan for it: browsers open up to six connections per host and often fetch `/favicon.ico` on their own. Serve `/favicon.ico` (or a 204) as one more static path, and give static GETs their own pool so a page load cannot starve the four unauthenticated slots that `/pair` and `/info` need. If the owner's network shows the opposite, nothing changes in the build.

**U5. Whether a browser retries a connection the host drops past the pool (`src/adapters/remote.rs:701`).**
- Not searched with a result. Plan: the page shows "host busy, retrying" on a failed `fetch` and retries with backoff.

**U6. Back-forward cache and session-restore retention of the `?code=` URL (see 12).** Build to: single-use code, five-minute window, `no-referrer`, `replaceState` first.

**U7. `Sec-Fetch-Site` on WebSocket handshakes, and Safari/Chrome secure-context treatment of an IP-literal https origin** (needed for `crypto`, service workers, `Secure` cookies). Not found. The page uses none of the secure-context-only APIs, so nothing in the plan depends on it.

## For the owner

**O1. On the iPhone, does Safari open the QR's https URL from the Camera app, show a certificate warning with a "visit this website" path, and then (a) load the page, (b) open the events socket?**
- Favourable (a and b): the socket is used. Unfavourable on (b) (expected, per 8): the page polls and the plan documents "trust the certificate on this device" as the path to live updates.
- Works in both cases: build REST polling first, the socket as an upgrade.

**O2. Is the address `local_address()` picks the one the phone reaches (several interfaces, a VPN)?**
- Favourable: one address in the URL. Unfavourable: the plan lists every candidate interface address in the pairing window, as the JSON `addresses` field already allows, with the URL for the first and the rest shown as text.
- Works in both cases: the list.

**O3. Is one click-through the only trust step acceptable for a `control`-scope phone on the home network?**
- Favourable: the dialog says so. Unfavourable: the certificate download route, with a `read` default scope for a browser device. Works in both cases: pairing scope is chosen in the window, so default a browser to `read` and let the owner raise it.

I wrote the facts file at `/Users/sbgragent/Library/Application Support/Dispatch/tickets/299903e5/facts/1/repo/facts.md`. It is 1,406 words, no spike was run, and `git status` is empty.

The finding that most shapes the plan is about Safari. It does not apply a certificate click-through to `wss://`. WebKit bug 158345 is still open and Cockpit documents it. So the page must work over plain REST polling, with the events socket as an upgrade only where the browser lets it open. Trusting the certificate on the device (the issue's "download it" route) is what would give Safari a socket.

The file has 11 settled items, 7 unresolved items and 3 owner questions. Besides the Safari finding, the settled items cover:
- **WebSocket headers:** a browser WebSocket cannot set headers, and a subprotocol-carried token needs the host to echo the protocol back.
- **Refused upgrades:** a script cannot see why an upgrade was refused, so "revoked" has to come from a `fetch` 401 with its own error code.
- **Origin check:** browsers always send `Origin` on a WebSocket handshake, so the host must check it. Cookies are shared across ports, so `SameSite` alone does not protect a cookie-carried token.
- **No token in a URL:** this is the repo's own rule, not a standard.
- **Certificate SAN:** Chrome needs an IP subject alternative name on the certificate. The click-through still works without one.
- **Smaller points:** the Content-Security-Policy `connect-src` quirk in Safari, iPad Safari's Mac user agent, and Chrome's Local Network Access prompt.

Several browser questions had no usable source. I could not find anything on cookie storage after a click-through, an unprompted `/favicon.ico` request, or whether `history.replaceState` clears the code from the back-forward cache and Referer. Each of those lines gives the plan something to build whichever way it turns out.

The owner questions are about the iPhone Camera and Safari flow, whether `local_address()` picks the address the phone reaches, and whether one click-through is enough trust for a `control`-scope phone.
